items.title: Why Some People Love Hugs While Others Hate Them
items.snippet: Why do some hugs stay with us while others fade away? A survey of more than 15,000 UK adults published in PLOS One shows that 70% remember hugs for comfort, with empathy, relationship attachment styles, and body perception dictating how touch is stored in memory.

items.title: Nearly Half of Distressed Adults Use AI for Therapy
items.snippet: Are chatbots becoming informal therapists? A new study reveals that nearly half of adults experiencing severe psychological distress turn to generative AI tools for emotional support, raising urgent questions about clinical safety.

items.title: Breathing “Thin Air” May Protect Against Parkinson’s
items.snippet: Can breathing thin mountain air help Parkinson's patients? Researchers demonstrated that 39 minutes of controlled intermittent hypoxia safely lowers stress hormones, raises anti-inflammatory adiponectin, and protects BDNF levels without disturbing sleep.

items.title: Developing Fetal Brain Weeds Out Genetically Flawed Neurons
items.snippet: Why does the prenatal brain overproduce millions of neurons only to eliminate them? A landmark Nature study led by Harvard Medical School and Boston Children’s Hospital shows that the developing brain uses competitive synaptic pruning to weed out neurons carrying abnormal DNA mutations.

items.title: Brain Scans Fail to Predict How Well Individuals Regulate Emotions
items.snippet: A 2,175-person study led by CIMH reveals prefrontal cortex activation does not reflect how well an individual regulates emotions via cognitive reappraisal.

items.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
items.snippet: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.
